accroche: A pianist sits down, closes the lid, opens it slightly three times to mark the end of each movement, without playing a note in four minutes thirty-three seconds.
contenu_vulgarise:
On August 29, 1952, at the Maverick Concert Hall in Woodstock, New York, the pianist David Tudor sits down at his instrument to premiere a work by the American composer John Cage. He closes the keyboard lid to mark the beginning of the piece, consults a stopwatch, then opens it slightly a little later to mark the end of the first movement. He does it twice more, closing the lid for each new movement and opening it slightly to mark its end. In all, four minutes and thirty-three seconds will have elapsed without his pressing a single key.

The audience, who came for a contemporary piano recital, expects a piece like any other. Yet the score does exist: the first version, now lost, used conventional musical notation to indicate three periods of silence; a later version, held at MoMA in New York, represents the four minutes thirty-three seconds by a series of vertical lines.

## What Happens During the Silence

Cage would himself recount what could be heard that evening, in a hall whose walls were largely open to the surrounding forest: the wind stirring the trees during the first movement, the rain that had begun to drum on the roof during the second, and during the third, the spectators themselves, who produced all kinds of interesting sounds as they talked or left the hall.

This is precisely what the piece lets us hear: not an absence of sound, but everything that ordinarily passes for silence because we do not listen to it as music. Cage had already experimented, in 1951, with the anechoic chamber at Harvard University, a room designed to absorb all outside sound, and had found there that he continued to hear two sounds, one high and one low: the engineer in charge explained to him that these were his nervous system and the circulation of his own blood. Total silence, he concluded, does not exist.

## What This Shifts

4'33" does not merely defy the expectations of a concert, it undoes the idea that there is a hierarchy between the sounds that count as music and those that are ignored. Every performance of the piece is necessarily different from the last, since it depends entirely on what happens, beyond the composer's control, in the hall where it is played. What Tudor performed that August evening in 1952 is thus never played the same way twice, even though its score does not change by a single note.

carte.punch: A pianist plays no note for four minutes thirty-three seconds, and that is the whole piece.
carte.idee: In 1952, David Tudor premieres John Cage's 4'33": seated at the piano, he presses no key for four minutes thirty-three seconds. What we hear is the wind, the rain on the roof, then the audience itself. Every performance is necessarily different.

quiz.question: What is John Cage trying to show by composing a piece in which the performer plays no note for four minutes thirty-three seconds?
choix: That no sound deserves to be called music until a composer has written it on a score
That complete silence exists and that music must learn to approach it
That ambient sounds, ordinarily ignored, can be heard as music on a par with played notes
That keyboard instruments are less expressive than wind instruments for conveying emotion
quiz.explication: Cage does not claim that no sound counts as music until it is written down, nor that total silence exists: his experience in the anechoic chamber had convinced him of the opposite. What the piece lets us hear is the ambient sounds ordinarily ignored, the wind, the rain, the audience, bringing them within the frame of musical listening.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when does David Tudor's premiere of 4'33" take place?
choix: On August 29, 1952, at the Maverick Concert Hall in Woodstock
On August 29, 1952, at Carnegie Hall in New York
On August 29, 1952, at the Morgan Library in New York
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The premiere takes place on August 29, 1952, at the Maverick Concert Hall in Woodstock, New York, as reported by MoMA, which holds the score.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Cage himself recount having heard during the three movements of the piece, at Woodstock?
choix: Complete silence, which he judged finally achieved
The wind in the trees, the rain on the roof, then the noises of the audience
Only anticipatory applause from the impatient audience
Recordings played quietly by the organizers
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cage would recount having heard the wind stirring the trees during the first movement, the rain drumming on the roof during the second, and the spectators themselves during the third.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Cage discover in 1951, in the anechoic chamber at Harvard University, designed to absorb all outside sound?
choix: That no sound is ever perceptible there, confirming the existence of total silence
That the chamber, on the contrary, amplifies outside noises instead of absorbing them
That he continues to hear two sounds, produced by his own body
That only low sounds remain audible there, never high ones
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cage hears two sounds there, one high and one low; the engineer in charge explains to him that these are his nervous system and the circulation of his own blood. Total silence, Cage concludes, does not exist.
